title: Do In-Loop Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen paired design (N = 300 matched intents; 150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM generation per pair, replayed to both arms), the run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Both arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate for every paired intent (contingency n11 = 300; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired risk-difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because validators never flagged violations, no repair calls were invoked and the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was untestable in this run. We present the compact, artifact-grounded results and interpretive diagnostics (including a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate), describe how key design choices (shared generation semantics, adversary strength, verifier family, repair budget) determined inferential power, and release the preregistration and execution artifacts to support targeted follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: LLMs can automate intent-driven network configuration, but operators worry that generated artifacts may expand attack surface or otherwise introduce security-relevant regressions. Prior surveys and system work therefore recommend constrained generation, execution oracles, and GVR loops that iterate generation and verifier-guided repair [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. We designed, preregistered, and executed a narrowly scoped confirmatory experiment to answer one operational question: does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistered paired design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and deterministic Dockerized execution; (2) a compact, artifact-grounded report of the degenerate confirmatory outcome (no validator-detected violations in either arm across N = 300 pairs) together with exact numerical summaries; (3) concise methodological diagnostics clarifying why the primary confirmatory hypothesis was untestable in this run; and (4) artifact-grounded operational recommendations for follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise verifier-triggered repair.
sections.related_work: Three strands of verified literature frame this study. First, execution-guided or verifier-feedback architectures have improved correctness for code and IaC tasks by using verifier signals to direct repair; such systems demonstrate that verifier capability and repair strategies are decisive for realized gains [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Second, surveys and NetOps systems document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators or human oversight for operational deployments [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulation and testbed work shows that execution-based validation is feasible for research evaluations but cautions about external-validity gaps when porting to production devices [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. These records motivated a preregistered, deterministic paired test combining an emulator, deterministic validators, and a controlled adversarial-variant generator; the present experiment occupies the narrow niche of preregistered paired evaluation with archived per-episode verifier traces.
sections.methodology:
Design summary and preregistration: The preregistered design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) fixed a paired binary experiment with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents producing forbidden reachability). Primary inference: exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). CIs: bootstrap percentile method (final analysis used 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729; change recorded in analysis log). Sampling, deduplication, and contamination handling followed preregistered rules (exact duplicates removed; fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15 excluded). All preregistration fields are archived in the evidence bundle.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To conserve provider budget under the adapter contract we preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each matched intent a single LLM candidate is generated and that same candidate is replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This yields model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs and is recorded in the provider-call audit. Because baseline is a replay rather than an independent draw, between-arm independent-sample variance is reduced; we state this effect explicitly because it directly impacts the ability of a paired test to observe discordant pairs suitable for assessing repair efficacy.

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = the shared initial candidate replayed directly. Guarded = same initial candidate passed to deterministic validators; if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate, a single repair LLM call is permitted (max one repair per pair) under the preregistered repair policy. Repair prompts and the invocation rule are archived; across the run no repair prompt was issued because validators never reported forbidden reachability.

Validators and forbidden-reachability predicate (concise technical definition): We used two deterministic validators: (i) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that applies the emulator’s routing and ACL semantics to compute post-configuration reachability traces, and (ii) a lightweight static graph-based reachability analyzer that computes route/ACL-induced reachability under the same device-profile model. The forbidden-reachability predicate is a boolean property that evaluates to true if a candidate configuration causes at least one reachability relation that was previously disallowed by the task's policy model to become permitted (i.e., the configuration enables traffic from a protected or otherwise forbidden source to reach protected destinations per the emulator's policy and route semantics). Per-episode validator outputs record the validators’ judgment and the 'repair_applied' flag; the concise definition above is sufficient to interpret reported violations while full validator logic is archived in per-episode validator_trace artifacts.

Execution environment and determinism: The experiment executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation with deterministic orchestration and fixed sampling seeds. Two deterministic validators were combined with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports forbidden reachability. Provider-call and execution accounting (planned episodes = 600; completed = 600; failed = 0; model_calls_used = 300) are recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run executed the preregistered workload from 2026-08-28T22:15:28Z to 2026-08-28T22:50:41Z (execution manifest). Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the provider-call audit records 'shared_initial_generation' = 300 and model_calls_used = 300 (maximum_model_calls allowed by contract = 600).

Primary confirmatory outcome (compact statistical summary): Every paired intent passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms: baseline_success_count = 300, guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency: n11 = 300; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0 (see Table 1). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no discordant pairs were observed, the paired McNemar test is uninformative for repair efficacy in this run. A descriptive one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation probability computed from observing 0/300 violations is ≈ 0.00994; this numeric bound quantifies the maximum baseline violation rate consistent with the observed data at 95% confidence under simple binomial assumptions.

Repair activity and verifier concordance: Validators never signaled forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; consequently no repair calls were invoked and all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false. The two validators’ outputs were concordant on every episode; verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in archived analysis artifacts. Representative per-task artifacts (responses and scoring JSON) illustrate medium- and hard-difficulty patterns where the shared candidate matched the reference and validators reported no violations.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory hypothesis was untestable here: Two coupled design facts rendered the preregistered repair-efficacy hypothesis untestable in this run. First, shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally reduced model-call costs by replaying a single LLM candidate to both arms; this choice reduces between-arm sampling variance and the chance of observing a discordant violating candidate that repair could correct. Second, for the chosen model (declared: gpt-5-mini), task set, programmatic adversary generator, and deterministic validators, the initial candidates never violated the forbidden-reachability predicate. The combination produced a degenerate contingency (n11 = 300) with no discordant pairs; a McNemar paired test therefore provides no information about the ability of verifier-guided repair to rescue violations. This conclusion is not a null proof of verifier uselessness—rather, it clarifies that the run tested whether inserting a verifier changes compliance when baseline generation is already compliant under the chosen contract.

Operational and experimental lessons (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics vs inferential power: shared replay conserves model calls (model_calls_used = 300) but reduces independent draws needed to produce discordant violations; experiments intended to exercise repair efficacy should use independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or increase sample size and repair budgets. (2) Adversary potency matters: the programmatic adversarial generator used here did not produce validator-detectable violations; stronger or targeted adversaries against verifier predicates are needed to stress repair mechanisms. (3) Verifier family and oracle strength: repair efficacy depends on verifier detection power; including diverse, production-grade oracles would expand construct validity. (4) Reproducibility practice: deterministic orchestration and archived per-episode validator traces permit exact auditing of the degenerate outcome and support targeted follow-up designs—they are therefore an enabling artifact for iterative scientific refinement.

Threats to validity (concise, artifact-referenced): Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope limit the experiment’s internal ability to test repair efficacy (execution/model_configuration.json; deterministic_reconciliation.json). Construct validity: the forbidden-reachability predicate as implemented depends on the emulator’s policy and route semantics and on validator algorithms (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0'); archived validator_traces enable external assessment. External validity: tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized emulation; results do not directly generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic. Conclusion validity: degenerate contingency violates design-stage power assumptions and precludes confirmatory inference about repair efficacy; we therefore present the Clopper–Pearson descriptive bound and artifact-backed diagnostics rather than claiming evidence of repair effects.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline under a conservative shared_initial_candidate contract and deterministic validators. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on every pair (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised and the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was untestable in this design. The principal scientific yield of this run is precise, deterministic execution accounting, a tight descriptive upper bound on undetected baseline violations (≈0.00994 at one-sided 95%), and operationally relevant design diagnostics that guide follow-up stress tests (independent draws, stronger adversaries, larger repair budgets, and more diverse verifiers). We release the preregistration and per-episode artifacts to enable reproducible follow-up work specifically targeted to exercise verifier-triggered repair paths rather than to repeat the present degenerate outcome.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
